consensus_summary: The consensus views 'tree' as a polyvalent symbol with multiple distinct meanings depending on context, most prominently denoting a righteous person, eternal life (the Tree of Life), the cross of Christ, earthly kingdoms, and the nation of Israel.
book_summary: The book defines 'tree' as a single, scalable model of rooted covenant life that grows from an individual seed or person into a lineage, people, or nation, with branches representing members and fruit providing seed for further growth.
consensus_core_identification: Multiple distinct referents: individual believer, eternal life, the cross, earthly kingdoms, and the nation of Israel.
book_core_identification: A scalable covenant entity (person, lineage, or nation) known by its fruit and growing to shelter members.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus treats the individual, national, and kingdom meanings of 'tree' as distinct and separate symbolic applications. The book unifies these specific referents into a single scalable continuum of covenant life, while omitting the consensus's prominent Christological (the cross) and eschatological (Tree of Life) associations from its core definition.
material_contradiction: There is no direct contradiction; rather, the book synthesizes several discrete categories recognized by the consensus (believer, kingdom, Israel) into one cohesive, fractal definition of growth and lineage.
rationale: The book refines the consensus by proposing an underlying structural unity to the symbol. It takes what the consensus sees as scattered, polyvalent uses (a person bearing fruit, a mustard seed becoming a kingdom, a cedar representing an empire, an olive tree representing Israel) and defines them all as instances of the same scalable pattern of rooted life.
strongest_objection: By unifying 'tree' around the organic growth of a covenant people or lineage, the book's definition struggles to accommodate the very common biblical use of 'tree' (xylon) for the dead wood of the cross of Christ, and may underplay the unique ontological status of the Tree of Life.
